about: Conformance vectors for RFC 8785 JCS number serialization, covering the areas Appendix B does not.
generated_against: rfc8785 (Python) 0.1.4, cross-checked against V8 22.22.2 and an independent formatter written from ECMA-262 7.1.12.1
input_encoding_note: Double inputs are given as IEEE 754 big-endian hex, following the convention of RFC 8785 Appendix B, so a vector does not depend on the parser that reads it. The literal is a convenience and is not authoritative.

settled.name: upper-threshold-last-positional
settled.why: ECMA-262 7.1.12.1 uses positional notation while the decimal exponent is at most 21. This is the largest double below 1e21 and the value named in the thread.

settled.name: upper-threshold-first-exponential
settled.why: The next representable step up crosses into exponential form. The pair is the whole boundary; either alone tests nothing.

settled.name: upper-positional-1e20
settled.why: Well inside positional. Guards against an implementation that switches to exponential too early, which is what Python's own repr does at 1e16.

settled.name: upper-positional-1e16
settled.why: Python repr gives 1e+16 here. An implementation built on the host language's float repr fails this one and passes almost everything else.

settled.name: lower-threshold-last-positional
settled.why: Positional while the exponent is at least -6. 1e-6 is the last positional value at the small end.

settled.name: lower-threshold-first-exponential
settled.why: First value that goes exponential at the small end, and the first place a leading zero can appear in the exponent.

settled.name: exponent-no-leading-zero-single-digit
settled.why: Appendix B does not cover the exponent's leading zero. A formatter that pads to two digits emits 1.5e-07 here.

settled.name: exponent-no-leading-zero-1e-9
settled.why: Second single-digit negative exponent, so a padding bug is not mistaken for an off-by-one at the threshold.

settled.name: exponent-two-digit-negative
settled.why: Three-digit exponent, no padding question. Present so a failure on the single-digit cases is isolated to padding.

settled.name: exponent-two-digit-positive
settled.why: Positive exponents carry a plus sign and no leading zero.

settled.name: negative-zero
settled.why: JCS emits 0 for negative zero. An implementation that round-trips through a naive formatter emits -0.

settled.name: simple-fraction
settled.why: Shortest round-trip, not the exact binary value. Guards against an implementation printing 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.

admission_profile.name: safe-integer-admission
admission_profile.status: proposed on OpenSecureAIAlliance/RFCs#18; not adopted by the working group
admission_profile.rule: Every integer-valued JSON number in an evidence object, whatever its spelling or the host's numeric type, lies within -9007199254740991 to 9007199254740991. A verifier that finds one outside that range rejects the object before canonicalizing it. Numbers that are not integer-valued are outside this rule. Since every double of magnitude 2**53 or more is integer-valued, the rule admits no JSON number of that magnitude.
admission_profile.why_separate_from_the_serializer_suite: A serialization vector says what bytes RFC 8785 produces for a value. An admission case says whether an evidence profile accepts that value at all. Six of the fourteen settled vectors serialize correctly and are not admissible here, so a serializer test passing is not evidence that the profile admits the input.
admission_profile.reference_check: Parse the token exactly (a decimal, not a double), test whether the value is an integer, then test the range. The runner does this. An implementation that parses to a double first still gets every case in this file right, because each rejected value stays rejected after rounding; the exact parse is so the expectations are stated on the value the producer wrote.

cases.name: boundary-positive
cases.why: Largest safe integer. Admitted.

cases.name: boundary-negative
cases.why: Smallest safe integer. Admitted.

cases.name: two-to-the-53
cases.why: First integer above the range. Rejected. Under a bound of 2**53 a double-only verifier would admit it.

cases.name: two-to-the-53-negative
cases.why: Symmetric with the case above. Rejected.

cases.name: two-to-the-53-plus-one
cases.why: Parses to the same double as 2**53. Rejected, and a verifier cannot tell it from the case above after parsing, which is the point of the bound.

cases.name: two-to-the-68
cases.why: Appendix B note (2)'s value. Rejected; carry it as a string.

cases.name: spelling-with-fraction-zero
cases.why: Same value as 2**53 with a different spelling. Rejected. The token's spelling does not decide admission; its value does.

cases.name: spelling-exponent
cases.why: Same value as 2**53 in exponent form. Rejected.

cases.name: spelling-exponent-negative
cases.why: Negative counterpart. Rejected.

cases.name: in-range-with-fraction-zero
cases.why: Integer-valued, in range, spelled with a fraction. Admitted: value, not spelling.

cases.name: one-e-sixteen
cases.why: Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected. Serializes fine under RFC 8785, which is why the serializer suite and this suite are separate.

cases.name: one-e-twenty
cases.why: Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected.

cases.name: upper-threshold-last-positional
cases.why: The settled vector at the positional threshold. Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected.

cases.name: one-e-twenty-one
cases.why: Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected.

cases.name: one-e-hundred
cases.why: Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected.

cases.name: max-double
cases.why: Integer-valued double above the range. Rejected.

cases.name: fraction-half
cases.why: Not integer-valued. This rule does not reach it; admitted. Its bytes are the serializer suite's business.

cases.name: fraction-twelve-and-a-half
cases.why: Not integer-valued. Admitted.

cases.name: small-exponent
cases.why: Not integer-valued. Admitted.

cases.name: negative-zero
cases.why: Integer-valued, in range. Admitted.

observations_on_conformant_serialization.note: These were the pending cases before the admission profile existed. They record what shipped implementations do with out-of-range integers under RFC 8785 itself; the admission profile above is what settles them.

cases.name: integer-at-safe-range-boundary
cases.why: Largest safe integer. Both the spec and rfc8785 0.1.4 accept it, so it is the control for the pair below.

cases.name: integer-just-above-safe-range
cases.why: First integer above the safe range. RFC 8785 Appendix B note (1) says values meant as true integers SHOULD sit inside the range but that how a number is used does not affect the algorithm, so the spec serializes it. rfc8785 0.1.4 raises IntegerDomainError instead.

cases.name: integer-2-to-the-68
cases.why: The value in Appendix B note (2). 2**68 is a power of two, so the double is exact; what changes is the spelling: the shortest decimal that round-trips to that double is 295147905179352830000, and read back as an integer it is 4144 short of 295147905179352825856. That is not a floating-point loss. It is the reason an exact integer of this size belongs in a string, per Appendix D. rfc8785 0.1.4 refuses it.

cases.name: adjacent-integers-share-a-leaf
cases.why: The case that decides the question. 9007199254740992 and 9007199254740993 are distinct integers. Under ECMA-262 number serialization both canonicalize to 9007199254740992, so two different evidence objects produce identical canonical bytes and identical leaf hashes. Verified in V8 22.22.2 and in Node 24 / V8 13.6. The output is 2**53, just outside the safe range, which is why a bound of 2**53 - 1 rejects both parsed values and a bound of 2**53 admits both. rfc8785 0.1.4 refuses both inputs and therefore does not produce the collision, which means the deviating implementation is the fail-closed one and the conformant implementation is not.
cases.expect_per_spec: both canonicalize to {"agent_id":"a","seq":9007199254740992}, leaf 3f9d3e6edd300dd569ec99916ec6270597c7b07cea1602f4ce5216b01bac65ff for both

cases.name: conformant-serialization-of-an-integer-uses-a-double
cases.why: Appendix B note 2 settles what the algorithm does: even where an integer like 2**68 could be regarded as having extended precision, the serialization does not take that into consideration. It is a double. So there is one conformant answer and it is the one with the hazard in it, which is what note 1's SHOULD on producers is protecting against. A SHOULD on producers does not protect a verifier. Two shipped implementations get this wrong in opposite directions: rfc8785 0.1.4 refuses and so never produces the collision, making the deviating implementation the fail-closed one, while a big-integer language that skips the conversion prints the exact value and diverges silently from a conformant implementation on the same object. Neither of those two raises. Both produce well-formed canonical bytes. The leaf hashes differ.

input.context: as a field value in an evidence object, for example a duration or a byte count

observed.implementation: conformant: convert to a double, per ECMA-262 7.1.12.1, for example V8
non-conformant: a big-integer language that skips the conversion, for example Python int

cases.note: No answer asserted. What to do about a conformant collision is a question for the working group, not something a vector set should encode quietly.

how_this_set_was_checked.method: Each vector was run against eight plausible-but-wrong serializers. A vector that no wrong implementation fails is not evidence and was not kept.
how_this_set_was_checked.result: All 14 settled vectors fail at least one. Counts per wrong implementation: {'host-language-repr': 8, 'exponent-padded-to-two': 8, 'negative-zero-passthrough': 8, 'json-dumps-default': 8, 'exponent-without-plus': 11, 'exact-binary-expansion': 12, 'subnormal-flushed-to-zero': 9, 'precision-15-significant': 10}
how_this_set_was_checked.reference: Every expected value is the output of rfc8785 (Python) 0.1.4, not a hand-written expectation.
oracles: V8 22.22.2, named as a reference implementation in RFC 8785 section 3.2.2.3
an independent formatter written from ECMA-262 section 7.1.12.1
how_this_set_was_checked.oracle_agreement: All three agree on all 14 settled vectors. The one Appendix B entry available, 4430000000000000, is reproduced by all three.
